subject: reading
questionText: The passage primarily follows Nessa as she:
choices: overcomes nervousness through the conductor’s public praise
assumes the absent principal cellist’s continuing responsibilities
begins participating despite continuing to feel nervous
helps another player instead of joining the difficult passage
explanation: Nessa still has cold hands and chooses the last chair on Friday, but she prepares to play and later marks another player’s music. Participation grows without a disappearance of anxiety. The conductor gives a brief nod rather than public praise, the principal’s absence does not establish a continuing leadership role, and the pencil request follows rather than substitutes for her willingness to play.

passage.title: The Seat at the End
passage.context:
For three evenings, Nessa arrived early at the community orchestra and put her cello beside the last chair. From there she could follow the principal cellist's bow without anyone watching her own. When the conductor asked for volunteers to play a short phrase alone, she bent to tighten a string that was already tight.

On Thursday, the principal cellist was absent. A man who usually played beside Nessa began the phrase, stopped, and asked which note followed the rest. Nessa answered before she could decide whether to speak. He asked her to play the measure. She did, quietly, and then again so that the players behind them could hear. The conductor nodded and resumed rehearsal without comment.

Nessa expected to feel transformed on Friday. Instead, her hands were as cold as ever when she opened the case. She still chose the last chair. But when the conductor reached the difficult passage, she set her bow on the string instead of looking down at the pegs. Afterward, the man beside her asked if she would mark the tricky measure in his music. She took his pencil. Its point was blunt, so she traced the note twice.

subject: reading
questionText: Why does Nessa first tighten her string?
choices: She is preparing to accept the solo invitation
She is correcting the principal cellist’s tuning
She is avoiding volunteering to play alone
She wants the neighboring player to hear better
explanation: The string is already tight, and Nessa bends over it precisely when the conductor asks for volunteers. The unnecessary adjustment lets her avoid attention. Readiness would require an actual tuning need, no prior tuning by the principal is described, and playing for the neighboring player happens later, after the principal’s Thursday absence.

outlined before writing

questionText: The statement that Nessa’s hands are “as cold as ever” mainly serves to:
choices: cast doubt on whether Thursday’s measure was played accurately
make her participation seem dependent on the principal’s absence
qualify the idea that one successful moment removes her anxiety

questionText: How does Nessa’s use of the pencil at the end relate to her handling of the string at the beginning?
choices: The later action helps another player, whereas the earlier action helps her avoid attention
Both small tasks let her contribute indirectly while avoiding any audible part in rehearsal

subject: reading
questionText: The passage mainly explores how an interviewer:
choices: replaces an inaccurate date with the more precise memory supplied by a daughter
separates private family memories from the factual records used in an exhibition
finds that stall ownership is more important to a history than earlier family work
recognizes that a question about beginnings can have more than one valid interpretation
explanation: Dev realizes that Suri means independent responsibility while her daughter remembers earlier involvement. Two legitimate meanings of beginning require two fields and the recorded explanation. He does not label one date inaccurate, separate family memory from the exhibition, or rank one stage as more important; he preserves both and shows why they belong.

passage.title: An Interview with Two Beginnings
passage.context:
For an oral history of the East Market, the interviewer, Dev, asked each vendor to begin with the first day they had worked there. Suri described opening her fruit stall after moving to the city in 1984. She remembered the green scales, the stiff lock, and her fear that she would miscalculate change. Dev entered 1984 in the box marked “arrival” on his form.

At the next interview, Suri’s daughter interrupted gently. Her mother had sold fruit in the same market long before she owned a stall, carrying a tray for an uncle on school holidays. Suri laughed. Of course she remembered the tray. But when Dev had asked when she began working, she had understood him to mean when she became responsible for the business. “Before the key was mine,” she said, “I was helping.”

Dev considered correcting the date. The form allowed only one year. Instead, he added a second field: first involvement, and then first independent business. He asked Suri to describe an afternoon with the tray. She recalled counting the coins into her uncle’s hand and getting to keep the bruised fruit that would not sell. Those details had not appeared in the first recording.

For the final exhibition, Dev included both accounts. He did not edit out the daughter’s interruption; he asked both speakers for permission to use it. Their exchange, he thought, made the meaning of “beginning” visible. A visitor reading only the two dates might see a contradiction. A visitor hearing the exchange could understand why both belonged to Suri’s history.

subject: reading
questionText: What does Dev do after learning about Suri’s work with the tray?
choices: He redefines arrival to mean only the earliest involvement
He asks the daughter to choose one replacement year
He adds fields distinguishing early involvement from independent business
He retains 1984 and leaves the tray story undated
explanation: Dev adds fields for first involvement and first independent business and asks Suri about the earlier tray work. He does not repurpose a single field or ask the daughter to settle on one year. The exhibition later includes two dates, so the earlier involvement is not left as a merely undated illustration of 1984.

questionText: Suri’s distinction between “helping” and having the key suggests that she regards beginning work chiefly in terms of:
choices: assuming responsibility for running the business
keeping earnings rather than handling another’s money
remembering afternoons rather than scattered childhood details
moving from holidays to a regular stall
explanation: Suri explicitly says she understood beginning work as becoming responsible for the business, symbolized by having the key. Getting earnings is not her stated criterion; as a helper she counts coins into her uncle’s hand and keeps bruised fruit. Neither memory maturity nor a contrast between holiday and regular schedules supplies the distinction she gives.

questionText: The phrase “Before the key was mine” mainly functions as:
choices: a date marker allowing Dev to replace the daughter’s less precise recollection
a judgment that owning the stall was more valuable than helping an uncle
a concrete image for the change in responsibility that shapes Suri’s answer

It supplies no precise earlier date, does not rank the value of helping versus owning, and does not indicate that her original answer was uncertain; the issue is what she understood the question to mean.

questionText: How does Dev’s choice for the exhibition develop the change he makes to his form?
choices: The form preserves two categories, and the recorded exchange explains why those categories are needed
The form distinguishes stages, but the exhibition asks visitors to choose which date counts as the beginning

subject: reading
questionText: The passage’s central argument is that the surviving handbook copies:
choices: establish that apprentices’ routine alterations weakened masters’ authority over workshop practice
reveal active judgment alongside prescribed obedience, without establishing whose judgments were typical
illustrate why incomplete ownership records make handwritten notes less informative than printed rules
show that practical innovations gradually replaced the handbook’s technical errors across workshops
explanation: The introduction prescribes obedience, while the marks preserve acts of comparison and adaptation. Unidentified writers and selective survival prevent attributing a typical practice to apprentices or tracing a general decline in masters’ authority. The author does not rank handwriting below print: the sources answer different questions. The undated correction also cannot establish a gradual sequence in which innovations displaced technical errors.

passage.title: The Apprentices’ Margins
passage.context:
The printer’s handbook of 1792 contains a stern introduction: an apprentice should follow the master’s method exactly, for variation produces waste. For a historian interested in how printing was taught, the sentence seems to promise a simple hierarchy. The master possesses knowledge; the apprentice receives it. Three surviving copies, however, complicate that arrangement.

In one copy, a reader has written an alternative way to set a difficult line of type. Beside it, another hand has added, “Quicker, unless the spacing is narrow.” A second copy contains a diagram correcting the handbook’s illustration of a press screw. The correction is not dated. It could record a later innovation, a local difference in equipment, or an error already recognized when the book appeared. In the third copy, an owner copied a recipe for ink from the handbook but reduced one ingredient and added the price of the resulting batch.

It would be tempting to call these marks proof that apprentices resisted their masters. Yet no marginal writer is identified as an apprentice. A master might have written the alternative method, and an apprentice might have copied it without ever using it. The surviving copies were retained by workshops that later became collections; unmarked or heavily damaged copies may have disappeared. The historian cannot infer how typical these readers were simply from their survival.

Still, those cautions do not return us to the introduction’s orderly picture. Whoever made the notes treated the printed directions as something to compare, adapt, or question. The handbook prescribed obedience; the marked copies preserve acts of judgment. These are not mutually exclusive facts. They belong to different kinds of evidence: one states an ideal of instruction, while the others show several encounters with the instructions.

subject: reading
questionText: Which uncertainty does the passage explicitly associate with the corrected press-screw diagram?
choices: Whether the same correction appears in the other two surviving copies
Whether the person who drew it also copied the altered ink recipe
Whether the corrected design was adopted throughout the workshops that retained the handbook
Whether the change reflects a later innovation, local equipment, or an earlier error
explanation: Because the press-screw correction is undated, the author explicitly offers three possibilities: a later innovation, different local equipment, or an error already known at publication. The other questions concern corroboration across copies, the identity of a writer, or widespread adoption. None is the specific uncertainty the passage lists for this correction, and the examples are described in different copies rather than linked to one annotator.

subject: reading
questionText: The author would most likely regard the claim “the marginal notes reveal what most apprentices actually did” as:
choices: well supported, provided that the unidentified writers altered instructions about several distinct parts of printing
plausible because consistent marks across surviving copies establish typical practice
premature only because the sequence of the annotations cannot yet be dated more precisely
insufficiently supported because the writers’ identities and the sample’s representativeness are unresolved
explanation: The writer would first need to know that the annotators were apprentices and that these selectively surviving copies represent a wider population. Altering several kinds of instruction does not establish either point, and repetition among retained copies cannot by itself correct survival bias. More precise dates could clarify one correction, but chronology alone would still leave authorship and typicality unresolved.

subject: reading
questionText: As used in “the handbook prescribed obedience,” “prescribed” most nearly means:
choices: laid down as a required standard
described as behavior commonly observed in workshops
anticipated as a likely outcome
passed along as optional advice
explanation: The introduction tells apprentices what they should do and warns that variation produces waste. "Prescribed" therefore means laid down as a required standard. Describing routine behavior would report what actually happened; anticipating an outcome would predict it. Calling the instruction optional advice weakens the demand to follow the master exactly. All three miss the distinction between a norm and observed compliance.

questionText: The third paragraph primarily serves to:
choices: limit the conclusions one might draw from the examples before retaining a narrower claim
show that readers’ technical corrections supplied more reliable guidance than the handbook’s original printed directions
attribute the differences among the annotations to equipment used in local workshops
explain why the retained copies can stand in for the missing workshop record
explanation: The third paragraph limits attribution and generalization: the writers are unidentified, a note need not record actual use, and surviving copies may be unrepresentative. The final paragraph then keeps the narrower claim that readers exercised judgment. No relative technical accuracy is established. Local equipment is one possible explanation for one correction, not an explanation of all notes, and selective survival argues against treating the copies as a representative replacement for the lost record.

For a historian interested in how printing was taught, the sentence seems to promise a simple hierarchy. The master possesses knowledge; the apprentice receives it. Three surviving copies, however, complicate that arrangement.

In one copy, a reader has written an alternative way to set a difficult line of type. Beside it, another hand has added, “Quicker, unless the spacing is narrow.” A second copy contains a diagram correcting the handbook’s illustration of a press screw. The correction is not dated. It could record a later innovation, a local difference in equipment, or an error already recognized when the book appeared. In the third copy, an owner copied a recipe for ink from the handbook but reduced one ingredient and added the price of the resulting batch.

It would be tempting to call these marks proof that apprentices resisted their masters. Yet no marginal writer is identified as an apprentice. A master might have written the alternative method, and an apprentice might have copied it without ever using it. The surviving copies were retained by workshops that later became collections; unmarked or heavily damaged copies may have disappeared. The historian cannot infer how typical these readers were simply from their survival.

Still, those cautions do not return us to the introduction’s orderly picture. Whoever made the notes treated the printed directions as something to compare, adapt, or question. The handbook prescribed obedience; the marked copies preserve acts of judgment. These are not mutually exclusive facts. They belong to different kinds of evidence: one states an ideal of instruction, while the others show several encounters with the instructions.

questionText: Which distinction best connects the introduction with the annotated copies?
choices: The introduction establishes common workshop practice, whereas the copies show exceptional departures from it
The introduction states a desired instructional relationship, whereas annotations preserve particular responses to directions
The introduction preserves an early teaching practice, whereas annotations document how workshops later adopted technical innovations
The introduction records masters’ instructions, whereas the annotations record apprentices’ independent experimentation
explanation: The introduction expresses a desired hierarchy; the annotations preserve particular responses to instructions. Neither establishes how common obedience or variation was, so the departures cannot confidently be called exceptional. Undated marks do not supply a secure sequence of later innovation. The writers are not identified as apprentices, and copying a method would not necessarily mean independently trying it.

subject: reading
questionText: The passage mainly describes how a library:
choices: uses volunteers to reduce the delay in checking returned books into its catalog
creates a browsing display and establishes its success from fewer staff assistance requests
responds to holiday readership by sorting returned books for different age groups
makes recently returned books easier to find and checks how the change is used
explanation: The shelf makes checked-in books physically findable, and the staff then use both request counts and observations to learn how readers use it. Check-in was already prompt; volunteers observe rather than process returns. Fewer requests do not capture unrequested browsing, and holiday observations are a proposed follow-up, not the reason for the original trial or an age-based sorting system.

passage.title: The Delivery Shelf
passage.context:
At the Hill Street library, returned books used to spend a day on carts behind the desk. Librarians checked them in promptly, but returning them to their shelves took longer. Readers sometimes searched in the right aisle for a book the catalog correctly described as available and still could not find it.

The staff tried a small change. Books checked in before noon went onto a clearly labeled delivery shelf near the entrance, arranged by the day of return. A reader could take one directly from that shelf. After three days, anything remaining there went to its usual location. The library did not buy more copies or hire another worker.

During the first month, staff recorded fewer requests to locate available books. That count did not reveal how many readers used the shelf without asking for help. To find out, volunteers observed the shelf during four two-hour periods. They saw several readers find a particular title and others browse books they had not planned to borrow. The manager kept the shelf, moved its label lower so children could read it, and asked volunteers to repeat the observations during a school holiday. A holiday might bring a different mix of readers; she wanted the arrangement to work for them as well.

questionText: What happens to a book that remains on the delivery shelf for three days?
choices: It waits until a reader borrows it
It returns to the check-in cart
It moves lower for children’s access
It goes to its usual location
explanation: The three-day rule sends remaining books to their usual locations. Leaving a book until someone takes it ignores that deadline, and sending it back to a cart substitutes the old system for the stated rule. The manager lowers the label, not the books or their destination.

questionText: The passage primarily traces:
choices: a comparison establishing faster movement as the reason warm samples produce more boundary crossings
a replay that lets a student correct for different organism types in the samples
the refinement of a measurement and the claims that can reasonably follow from it
a shift from counting a population to identifying individual organisms responsible for its activity
explanation: Imani redefines crossings as activity in a fixed area and limits her claims after considering alternative explanations. The study does not separate temperature effects from organism-type differences or identify the organisms involved. Replaying the video exposes a counting mismatch; it does not correct the sample-composition difference.

passage.title: A Window into the Pond
passage.context:
In the school laboratory, Imani watched a drop of pond water through a microscope. Small organisms crossed the circle of light, sometimes darting out of focus. She wanted to compare their movement at two temperatures. Counting every organism in the drop seemed impossible, so her teacher suggested filming a fixed square in the microscope’s view for one minute at a time.

Imani recorded the number of crossings of the square’s boundary. At the warmer temperature, there were more crossings. She began to write that warmer water contained more organisms. Then she replayed the video. One organism had entered the square, turned, left, and entered again. It contributed three boundary crossings without becoming three organisms.

She revised her question to ask about activity in the filmed area. To make the comparison more consistent, she used the same magnification and square size in every recording. She also allowed each sample to reach the target temperature before filming. These choices did not let her follow individual organisms throughout the drop, but they made the recorded action clearer to define.

When Imani presented the study, another student asked whether the organisms had moved faster because the water was warmer or because the samples contained different kinds of organisms. Imani could not distinguish those explanations with the videos she had. She added the question to her final slide. The teacher asked her to keep the slide there during discussion: identifying what the measure did not establish was part of understanding what it did.

subject: reading
questionText: Which condition does Imani keep the same across recordings?
choices: The magnification and size of the filmed square
The target temperature reached by each separate sample
The number of organisms entering the square each minute
The types of organisms in each water drop
explanation: Imani explicitly holds magnification and square size constant. She uses two temperatures and lets each sample reach its own target, rather than setting every sample to the same temperature. Crossing activity is measured rather than fixed, and the organism types remain a possible difference she cannot distinguish with the videos.

subject: reading
questionText: The passage’s central point is that:
choices: claims of service growth depend on which measure and comparison base are used
annual identifier resetting explains why the share of households using the centers declined
visits provide a more useful measure of household access than population estimates do
the centers’ increased workload indicates that residents’ unresolved needs became more complex
explanation: Visits and distinct visiting households increase, but the service-area estimate grows faster, reducing the share reached. Thus the claim changes with the measure and comparison base. Resetting identifiers prevents linking particular households across years; it does not cause the annual proportion to decline. The passage retains complementary measures rather than ranking visits above population estimates, and supplies no evidence about the complexity of unmet needs.

passage.title: A Changing Denominator
passage.context:
A city’s annual report announced that use of its neighborhood advice centers had increased. The statement was true in one sense: the centers recorded more visits. The report also said that “a growing proportion of local households is receiving help.” That second claim required information the visit totals did not supply.

The accompanying table separates visits, distinct households recorded as visiting, and households estimated to live in the service area. Staff assigned each visiting household an anonymous identifier, so repeat visits could be distinguished from first visits within a year. The identifiers were reset at the start of the next year, meaning the table could not show which households returned from one year to the next.

A researcher, Oren, noted that the share of households recorded as visiting had actually declined, even though both visits and distinct visiting households had risen. New housing had expanded the estimated service-area population more rapidly. The centers had served more households in absolute terms while reaching a smaller share of the enlarged population.

This did not establish that residents found the service less helpful. The table included no measure of satisfaction, whether a problem was resolved, or how many households needed advice. Nor did it show that any specific household had lost access. Oren recommended keeping the original statement about visits, replacing the proportional claim, and adding a separate study of unmet need. “The denominator is not an inconvenience,” he wrote. “It is part of the question.” The revised report retained all three columns rather than choosing the one that made the largest increase appear.

subject: reading
questionText: What do the annually reset identifiers prevent the table from showing?
choices: The number of distinct visiting households within a year
The number of visits recorded at the advice centers during each year
The estimated number of households in the service area
Which specific households returned from one year to the next
explanation: Reset identifiers cannot link a particular household in Year 1 with that household in Year 2. Within each year they still distinguish repeat from first visits, allowing the distinct-household count. The table also records visits and estimates the service-area population. Those annual totals remain available even though the identities behind totals cannot be followed across years.

A researcher, Oren, noted that the share of households recorded as visiting had actually declined, even though both visits and distinct visiting households had risen. New housing had expanded the estimated service-area population more rapidly. The centers had served more households in absolute terms while reaching a smaller share of the enlarged population.

This did not establish that residents found the service less helpful. The table included no measure of satisfaction, whether a problem was resolved, or how many households needed advice. Nor did it show that any specific household had lost access. Oren recommended keeping the original statement about visits, replacing the proportional claim, and adding a separate study of unmet need. “The denominator is not an inconvenience,” he wrote. “It is part of the question.” The revised report retained all three columns rather than choosing the one that made the largest increase appear.

questionText: The central change in Mateo’s perspective is that he:
choices: abandons close views so the bed’s function can be shown
values the beds after Ms. Bell agrees to remove untidy material
begins to consider a landscape’s function as well as its appearance
makes a useful camera angle the sole test of appearance
explanation: Mateo first wants a tidier composition but later keeps an overhead drainage view and a close view of a stalk and leaf. He is considering function as well as appearance. Keeping both views contradicts giving up visual interest, Ms. Bell removes a wrapper rather than all the stalks, and no single camera angle becomes the sole standard of judgment.

passage.title: Making Room for Rain
passage.context:
The new beds outside the school cafeteria looked unfinished to Mateo. Their edges curved instead of meeting at right angles, and dry stalks stood among the spring leaves. He had offered to photograph the campus for a brochure. He asked the groundskeeper, Ms. Bell, whether she could tidy the beds before he returned with his camera.

Ms. Bell handed him a folded plan. The beds were lower than the surrounding pavement so that rain could collect rather than rush into the street. The stalks were last year’s flowers; she was leaving some until the insects sheltering inside had emerged. Mateo admitted that a square bed would be easier to fit into his picture. “Water doesn’t choose its route for the brochure,” she said.

A storm interrupted their conversation. They watched from the doorway as shallow streams moved off the pavement. Water pooled among the stalks and then slowly disappeared into the soil. A plastic lunch wrapper remained caught on one stem. Ms. Bell put on boots to collect it.

The next morning, Mateo photographed the bed from above, including the pavement that sloped toward it. He also took the close view he had planned. In that one, a stalk cast a narrow shadow across a new leaf. He left both photographs in the brochure draft, with space underneath for a caption he had yet to write.

explanation: Ms. Bell explicitly leaves some stalks until the insects sheltering inside have emerged. The wrapper later catches on one stalk, but incidental litter catching is not her stated reason. subject: reading
questionText: The passages chiefly examine:
choices: how translators choose between preserving physical objects and retaining abstract meaning
why a shared interpretation requires translators to preserve the same line length
how different translation choices emphasize different aspects of the same poem
how agreement about a literal noun can coexist with different approaches to tone
explanation: The translators choose different nouns and lengths to emphasize different relationships among object, implication and hesitation. Neither treats physical and abstract meaning as an exclusive choice. They do not require one line length, and they use different English words rather than agreeing on a noun and disagreeing only about tone.

passage.title: Two Translations of a Doorway
passage.context:
Passage A — Translator’s note
The poem’s speaker addresses a doorway using a word that can refer to a physical threshold or to the beginning of an undertaking. My first translation used “entrance.” It was accurate in a narrow sense, but it sounded like a label on a building plan. I finally chose “threshold,” because the speaker is both standing at a door and hesitating before a decision. English lets the word hold those possibilities together. I kept the line short, although the source line is longer. A close copy of its length produced an unearned grandeur in English, making an intimate hesitation sound like a public declaration.

Passage B — A second translator’s note
I used “doorstep” for the same word. My aim was to keep the speaker’s shoes, the worn stone, and the domestic setting close to the reader. “Threshold” can carry an abstract significance before the poem has earned it. I do not deny that the doorway suggests a decision; I want that implication to arise from the speaker’s pause rather than from the noun alone. I kept the longer line, allowing its small qualifications to delay the final verb. For me, the length makes hesitation audible. Neither version can reproduce every relation among sound, object, and implication. The question is which relation a particular choice brings forward.

subject: reading
questionText: Why does the first translator reject the word “entrance”?
choices: It introduces abstract significance before the speaker’s pause can make it meaningful
It conveys a grandeur that the translator prefers to create through length
It emphasizes domestic detail so strongly that the decision implication is lost
It sounds too much like a literal label for the desired effect
explanation: The first translator says entrance is narrowly accurate but sounds like a building-plan label. That literal effect is insufficient. Concern about premature abstract significance belongs to B’s objection to threshold; A rejects rather than seeks grandeur, and the domestic surface is B’s reason for choosing doorstep, not A’s stated objection to entrance.

subject: reading
questionText: The passage primarily argues that the glacier’s dust bands:
choices: primarily record volcanic activity whose effects can be separated from the effects of summer warmth
are strongest as temperature measures when tree records agree, even if the dust’s source has not been investigated
can inform climate reconstruction when their sources and processes are considered alongside other evidence
date summer warmth more precisely than tree records through differences in mineral composition
explanation: The researchers use dust as one contribution to reconstruction, examining sources, interacting processes, and independent warmth estimates. Most bands resemble valley material, not volcanic deposits, and the passage does not claim cleanly separated effects. Agreement with trees does not make dust source irrelevant. Mineral resemblance investigates origin rather than providing a more precise date for summer warmth.

passage.title: The Dust between the Layers
passage.context:
A core removed from a mountain glacier contains thin bands of dark dust between layers of compressed snow. A team studying the core found several dust bands near layers whose chemistry suggested unusually warm summers. One account of the result described the dust as a “thermometer preserved in ice.” The phrase was vivid, but it collapsed several possible sequences into one.

Dust might have arrived during warm, dry weather that exposed bare ground downwind. It might also have arrived after an eruption or an unusually strong storm, neither of which required a warm summer at the glacier. Once deposited, dark material could absorb more sunlight than clean snow and contribute to melting. In that case, dust could be partly a consequence of regional conditions and partly an influence on the local ice surface. The possibilities were not exclusive.

To investigate the source, the team compared the bands’ mineral composition with samples from exposed valleys and volcanic deposits. Most bands more closely resembled valley material, but two had a different signature. The team also compared the sequence with nearby tree records that estimated summer warmth independently. Several broad peaks aligned; their dates were not precise enough to establish which event came first within a particular summer.

The researchers concluded that the dust bands could contribute to a reconstruction when interpreted alongside other evidence. They rejected using the darkness of a band as a direct reading of summer temperature. A pale layer did not prove a cold season, since ground cover and winds might have limited dust transport. A dark layer did not identify a single cause. The core preserved an intersection of processes, not a set of labels waiting to be read aloud.

subject: reading
questionText: Why could the tree records not establish which event came first within a summer?
choices: Their warmth peaks never aligned
Two mineral signatures remained unexplained
They measured warmth rather than deposition
Their dates lacked sufficient precision
explanation: The stated obstacle is that the dates are not precise enough to order events within a summer, despite broad alignment. Two unusual mineral signatures concern dust origin, not the dating precision of trees. A separate warmth record need not measure deposition directly to help establish sequence if dates are precise; here the passage specifically identifies insufficient temporal resolution as the limit.

questionText: Which new finding would most directly weaken the use of a pale layer as evidence of a cold summer?
choices: Evidence matching one unusual band’s mineral composition to a known volcanic deposit
Evidence that a dust-covered surface melts faster than nearby clean snow under the same sunlight
Evidence that thick vegetation prevented dust from leaving a valley during a warm summer

Matching a volcanic source and enhanced melting concern the interpretation of dust that is present. Dust transport in a cold summer would challenge the converse dark-equals-warm assumption, not directly show why a pale layer could form in a warm summer.

Dust might have arrived during warm, dry weather that exposed bare ground downwind. It might also have arrived after an eruption or an unusually strong storm, neither of which required a warm summer at the glacier. Once deposited, dark material could absorb more sunlight than clean snow and contribute to melting. In that case, dust could be partly a consequence of regional conditions and partly an influence on the local ice surface. The possibilities were not exclusive.

To investigate the source, the team compared the bands’ mineral composition with samples from exposed valleys and volcanic deposits. Most bands more closely resembled valley material, but two had a different signature. The team also compared the sequence with nearby tree records that estimated summer warmth independently. Several broad peaks aligned; their dates were not precise enough to establish which event came first within a particular summer.

The researchers concluded that the dust bands could contribute to a reconstruction when interpreted alongside other evidence. They rejected using the darkness of a band as a direct reading of summer temperature. A pale layer did not prove a cold season, since ground cover and winds might have limited dust transport. A dark layer did not identify a single cause. The core preserved an intersection of processes, not a set of labels waiting to be read aloud.

questionText: Together, the passages primarily consider:
choices: why an existing shortcut provides enough evidence for choosing the route
whether commuter convenience justifies opening a garden that should remain closed
why current users’ preferences should outweigh the needs of absent users
how to choose a useful path while considering different garden users
explanation: Both writers discuss choosing the route, with A emphasizing dependable access and B the needs of quieter users. Each identifies needs that visible foot traffic can miss. The trail is not sufficient evidence, B accepts a public route rather than demanding none, and A’s mud-avoiding potential users cannot be excluded from the decision.

passage.title: Who Takes the Shortcut?
passage.context:
Passage A — A pedestrian planner
A proposed walkway would connect Alder Court to the station through a corner of the public garden. Residents already cross the lawn there, leaving a narrow track. Paving that track could give people with wheeled bags a dependable surface and keep mud from spreading across the station entrance. I favor a route that curves around the oldest trees. Counting existing walkers is a useful start, but the count will not include people who avoid the muddy route today.

Passage B — A garden volunteer
I do not object to a public route through the garden. I object to choosing it solely by the trail that hurried commuters have already made. The quiet corner beside the pond is used for small classes, including a weekly group whose members walk slowly. Their activity leaves no worn track. Before deciding where to pave, the council should observe the garden at several times of day and ask people who use its quieter places. A short path is convenient, but convenience has more than one owner.

The council has funding for one accessible path. Both writers have been asked to comment before the route is selected. Neither writer proposes closing the garden or removing the station entrance.

choices: Counting walkers already using the muddy shortcut to estimate demand

Comparing the worn track’s length with the route around the pond
explanation: B explicitly asks for observations at several times of day and consultation with quiet-area users. Counting existing walkers and curving around old trees belong to A’s discussion, not B’s additional recommendation. B gives no proposal to compare measured route lengths; the concern is whose uses the visible track omits.

questionText: The passage mainly follows Leon’s growing recognition that:
choices: a remembered story supplies the complete visual portrait that the brief film cannot provide on its own
his aunt’s reluctance comes chiefly from knowing the film will disappoint his expectation of a portrait
a person’s presence can emerge through stories and actions as well as a clear image
the brief image gains value once Celia explains why his mother avoided appearing before the camera
explanation: Leon initially expects a clear image but ends by seeking the story of his mother arranging the plate: character emerges through remembered action too. The story does not supply a complete visual portrait, Celia’s precise motive is not confined to his expectations, and working behind the camera does not establish a wish to avoid appearing.

passage.title: The Unprojected Film
passage.context:
The film canister had sat on Aunt Celia’s hall table for a week before Leon asked what was inside. “A summer,” she said. The label gave a year, a place, and his mother’s name, but no description. Celia had borrowed a projector from the local club. Each evening she checked the plug, opened the canister, and put it back beside the machine.

Leon offered to thread the film. Celia said she knew how. She had shown it often when his mother was alive. Then she asked him to shut the curtains, although there was still an hour of daylight. He pulled them halfway and waited. Across the room, a bright strip lay on the empty screen.

Celia finally explained that the film included a picnic at which his mother had spent most of the afternoon behind the camera. There might be only a glimpse of her at the end. Leon had expected a clear image of someone he scarcely remembered. He wondered why a film with almost none of her in it mattered so much. Before he could ask, Celia described the impatient way his mother had called everyone into the frame, then moved a plate that spoiled the composition. Celia’s imitation made him laugh.

They watched the film that evening. The picture trembled; a dog crossed in front of the lens. At the end, the camera swung briefly toward his mother, too quickly for a still portrait. Afterward, Leon asked Celia to tell him again about the plate. She left the projector on the table, but put the canister’s lid underneath it so they would not lose it.

questionText: What does Celia say is likely to appear near the end of the film?

A brief glimpse of Leon’s mother
His mother posing after gathering everyone
His mother taking back the camera

questionText: The passages chiefly debate:
choices: whether the petition’s geographical details can establish the legal boundary of the common landing
whether the merchants’ purpose makes their map less reliable than other maps
whether an uncertain legal claim leaves room for evidence of shared practical use
whether evidence of everyday trade can explain why officials granted the merchants a shared legal right
explanation: A warns that the petition’s requested recognition is not proof of an established right. B accepts that limit but asks what the map, with further records, can reveal about practical use. Neither says geography alone fixes a legal boundary or compares the map’s reliability with other maps. No official response has been found, so a granted right cannot be treated as the premise of their debate.

passage.title: The Map in the Petition
passage.context:
Passage A — Historical geographer
A map attached to an 1810 petition shades a narrow strip beside the river and labels it “common landing.” Later historians have used the map to show that the landing belonged to everyone in the district. The petition’s authors were merchants seeking a road to the river. Their map certainly shows that they wanted officials to recognize a shared landing. It does not, by itself, establish an uncontested legal right. A petition presents a case. We should examine the records of neighboring landholders and the authorities’ response before turning its desired recognition into an accomplished fact.

Passage B — Historian of everyday commerce
The warning about legal title is sound, but it should not reduce the map to evidence of an unrealized wish. Merchants built an argument around a place that their readers were expected to recognize. The map locates warehouses, a ferry queue, and a route worn between them. Those details may reveal a shared working geography even if formal rights were disputed. I would compare the map with delivery records and references to tolls. Such evidence could tell us how people used the landing while the question of ownership remained unsettled. A place can function as common ground without being common property.

The surviving map does not name individual users. No official response to the petition has yet been located. Both historians distinguish the document’s claim from a final legal determination.

passage.title: The Map in the Petition
passage.context:

A map attached to an 1810 petition shades a narrow strip beside the river and labels it “common landing.” Later historians have used the map to show that the landing belonged to everyone in the district. The petition’s authors were merchants seeking a road to the river. Their map certainly shows that they wanted officials to recognize a shared landing. We should examine the records of neighboring landholders and the authorities’ response before turning its desired recognition into an accomplished fact.

The warning about legal title is sound, but it should not reduce the map to evidence of an unrealized wish. Merchants built an argument around a place that their readers were expected to recognize. I would compare the map with delivery records and references to tolls. Such evidence could tell us how people used the landing while the question of ownership remained unsettled. A place can function as common ground without being common property.

The surviving map does not name individual users. No official response to the petition has yet been located. Both historians distinguish the document’s claim from a final legal determination.

questionText: The passage mainly shows Lina working to:
choices: replace family wording with factual descriptions on the box
preserve an original label while clarifying what it means
identify which photographs the donor had dated incorrectly

explanation: Lina keeps the handwriting and quoted family expression while adding a factual description and an explanation. She clarifies rather than replaces the label. The date is never challenged, and the classroom’s request broadens after her explanation rather than requiring the archive’s descriptions to conform to the initial completed-boat request.

passage.title: A Record of the Workshop
passage.context:
When the town archive received a box of workshop photographs, the donor labeled them “finished boats, 1968.” The archivist, Lina, noticed that several pictures showed empty frames and scattered tools. She telephoned the donor, who explained that his father had called any boat being built “a finished boat waiting to happen.” It was a family expression, not a description of the construction stage.

Lina kept the donor’s words in quotation marks on the collection record. Beneath them she added a plain description of the images and a note explaining the expression. The donor offered to relabel the box himself, but Lina declined. The handwriting on the lid was part of the gift’s history, and a new label would make the origin of the phrase harder to trace.

A teacher later asked for photographs of completed boats for a classroom display. Lina sent two images and explained why she had not sent the others. The teacher then requested one picture of a frame as well. Her students could compare stages of work and discuss why the family’s label differed from an archivist’s description.

Before closing the box, Lina slipped a copy of their correspondence into the folder. The photographs had arrived with one description. They would leave the archive for the classroom with enough information to understand that description rather than simply repeat it.

questionText: The passage mainly describes Farah’s effort to:
choices: use wider feedback while avoiding claims that its totals cannot support
prioritize comments from residents who miss evening meetings
combine submissions from each household to give every household one recorded voice
compare which courtyard rules are most popular among users of different entrances
explanation: Farah uses the wider feedback but reports comments rather than people and considers the impact of uncommon access problems. The new channels permit participation without attendance, but she does not give those contributors priority. She explicitly declines to merge anonymous submissions into a head count. The entrance question is intended to locate problems, not to rank the popularity of rules by entrance.

passage.title: The Meeting after the Meeting
passage.context:
A housing association used to collect comments only at its monthly evening meeting. Minutes showed lively debate, yet the secretary, Farah, noticed that the same twelve names appeared repeatedly. When the association considered changing courtyard rules, it also distributed paper forms and opened an online comment page. Forms could be returned to a box by the lift, without attending the meeting.

The new channels produced eighty comments. Several described problems the committee had not discussed: a door that was difficult to push while carrying a child, and a noticeboard too high for some residents to read. The chair proposed calling the results “what residents want.” Farah hesitated. A comment was not necessarily a person; some residents had written online and on paper. Others had sent one form signed by several household members.

She did not try to merge the anonymous contributions into a head count. Instead, she organized them by issue and labeled the totals as comments. At the next meeting, she presented recurring concerns along with several uncommon ones that involved access. A rule supported by many comments could still create a serious obstacle for a smaller group.

The committee kept the evening meeting and the new channels. On the next forms, it asked people to indicate which courtyard entrances they used, without requesting their names. Farah wanted to learn whether a concern was concentrated around a particular entrance. She was seeking a better description of the problem, not a more impressive total.

questionText: The passage primarily explores the narrator’s:
choices: defense of a step count symbolizing the grandfather’s authority
reconciliation of family memories through a verified account of rebuilding
effort to distinguish remembered experience from an appealing but uncertain detail

explanation: The narrator keeps the remembered experience of carrying dishes but becomes cautious about the appealing number and even the pleasure of the revision. passage.title: The Number on the Door
passage.context:
I had always told the story with the number seventeen. Seventeen steps from the lane to my grandfather’s kitchen: I could count them in the dark, I said, because he had made me carry the supper dishes one at a time. My cousins remembered a shorter flight. They were younger, I reminded them. Childhood makes everything larger; perhaps it also makes counting unreliable.

When the house was sold, I went back to help clear it. Twelve steps rose from the lane. I counted twice, then noticed a pale line along the wall and decided that the lower steps must have been replaced. The new owner knew of no alteration. I pointed out that he had only recently arrived, an observation that did nothing to produce five missing steps.

Inside, the kitchen door bore a brass number seventeen, left from a time when the building had contained rented rooms. I remembered polishing that number with a corner of my apron while Grandfather waited for me to stop delaying supper. I also remembered the weight of a plate and my careful progress upward. For a moment I tried to make a single scene of those things, but the door and the stairway refused to stay in the right order.

I did not tell my cousins that I had solved the mystery. I had found another number, not a witness who could explain the first one. In the version I told at dinner, I kept the dishes and left the steps uncounted. One cousin said it was a better story. That pleased me, until I wondered whether pleasure was exactly what had made seventeen so durable.

questionText: The passage mainly describes students who:
choices: establish shade as the planter’s advantage and recommend that location for birds
test a possible explanation and choose wording that reflects the study’s limits
count distinct birds at two dishes and generalize to the rooftop population
replace an inconclusive comparison with a new study of water temperature
explanation: The students shade one dish to explore an explanation and then narrow their wording to the setting and limits of what they recorded. They count landings, not distinct birds, and neither plants nor other influences are ruled out. Water temperature is identified as unmeasured; it does not become the subject of a replacement study.

passage.title: The Rooftop Observers
passage.context:
A class installed two shallow water dishes on the roof outside its science room. One stood beside a planter, and the other stood two meters away on bare paving. Students watched from a window for fifteen minutes each morning. They recorded the number of birds that landed at each dish, not the number of different birds: an individual could leave and return during an observation.

At first the planter dish received more landings. Hana suggested that birds preferred being near plants. Her partner, Ellis, noticed that the planter also cast shade over its dish. They could not tell which feature mattered from those observations alone. The following week, with permission, they moved a screen to shade the dish on the paving. They left the planter dish and their observation time unchanged.

Landings at the newly shaded dish increased. Hana wanted to title the report “Shade attracts rooftop birds.” Ellis suggested “Landings at two rooftop dishes before and after a shade screen.” He agreed that the change was worth reporting, but pointed out that the class had watched only one roof and had not measured wind or water temperature. Hana shortened his title, kept the location in it, and added a drawing showing where the screen had stood. The class left the dishes in place for the next group of students.

questionText: What did the students count during each observation?
choices: The amount of water consumed at each dish
The number of distinct species on the roof
The number of landings at each dish
The number of different individual birds
explanation: The first paragraph states that students counted landings at each dish and that an individual could return. Distinct individuals are therefore not the same measure. Water consumption and species counts would be plausible observations of bird use, but the passage does not report collecting either.

subject: reading
questionText: The passage primarily describes a restoration team’s decision to:
choices: select the damaged border’s most likely pattern from comparable bathhouses
make an incomplete design visible without presenting a conjecture as established fact
complete the wall while postponing documentation of the uncertain missing corner
move the surviving fragments to a separate display before reconstructing the wall consistently
explanation: The team fills the gap with distinguishable tiles and displays two possible patterns, making the wall coherent while exposing what remains unknown. Similar buildings supply a possibility, not a pattern the team adopts as fact. Documentation is part of the completed repair, not a postponed task. The fragments remain in place under a clear covering rather than moving to a separate display.

passage.title: The Missing Blue Tiles
passage.context:
During repairs to a public bathhouse, workers uncovered part of a tiled wall beneath a later layer of plaster. Most tiles were white. A few blue fragments suggested a border, but a damaged corner gave no clear indication of how that border had turned. An early photograph showed the room from the opposite end, with the relevant wall blurred by steam.

The restoration team considered completing the border with new blue tiles. A continuous line would help visitors imagine the room when it was in use. Yet each proposed corner pattern required an assumption that neither the fragments nor the photograph could confirm. One designer suggested choosing the pattern most common in similar buildings. The historian objected that a common pattern was evidence of a possibility, not evidence that this bathhouse had used it.

They decided to fill the missing area with slightly lighter tiles and show two possible border patterns on a nearby panel. Seen from the entrance, the repair made the wall look whole. Up close, the lighter tiles marked where the evidence ended. The panel included a photograph of the fragments before repair and explained why the team had not selected a single reconstructed corner.

At the opening, a visitor complained that the wall looked uncertain. The historian agreed that it was. She had wanted a visitor to see both the surviving design and the boundary of the team’s knowledge. An uninterrupted blue line would have been easier to admire, she said, but harder to question. The fragments remained in place, protected beneath a clear covering, beside the lighter repair.

subject: reading
questionText: What feature allows a visitor standing near the wall to recognize the repaired area?
choices: The clear covering placed over the surviving blue fragments
The two alternative corner patterns shown on the nearby panel
The changes in the border visible in the early photograph
Tiles that are slightly lighter than the surviving ones
explanation: The passage directly says the slightly lighter tiles mark where the evidence ends when the wall is viewed up close. The clear covering protects original fragments, while the panel explains possible patterns; neither is the feature identified as marking the repaired area. The early photograph is blurred at the relevant wall and cannot supply a clear change in the border.

passage.title: The Missing Blue Tiles
passage.context:
During repairs to a public bathhouse, workers uncovered part of a tiled wall beneath a later layer of plaster. Most tiles were white. A few blue fragments suggested a border, but a damaged corner gave no clear indication of how that border had turned. An early photograph showed the room from the opposite end, with the relevant wall blurred by steam.

The restoration team considered completing the border with new blue tiles. A continuous line would help visitors imagine the room when it was in use. Yet each proposed corner pattern required an assumption that neither the fragments nor the photograph could confirm. One designer suggested choosing the pattern most common in similar buildings. The historian objected that a common pattern was evidence of a possibility, not evidence that this bathhouse had used it.

They decided to fill the missing area with slightly lighter tiles and show two possible border patterns on a nearby panel. Seen from the entrance, the repair made the wall look whole. Up close, the lighter tiles marked where the evidence ended. The panel included a photograph of the fragments before repair and explained why the team had not selected a single reconstructed corner.

At the opening, a visitor complained that the wall looked uncertain. The historian agreed that it was. She had wanted a visitor to see both the surviving design and the boundary of the team’s knowledge. An uninterrupted blue line would have been easier to admire, she said, but harder to question. The fragments remained in place, protected beneath a clear covering, beside the lighter repair.

subject: reading
questionText: The passage’s main concern is:
choices: whether a spoken reading should give readers the same physical experience as handling a notebook
how an audio edition can make its unavoidable interpretive choices available for inspection
how an actor can resolve uncertainty by faithfully performing every visible manuscript mark
why smooth readings more accurately represent authorial intention than readings that announce revisions
explanation: Both trial readings impose interpretation; the final edition makes significant choices inspectable through introductions, images, and a transcript that separates speech from marks. It does not recreate handling a notebook. Performing every mark still assigns timing, emphasis, and intention rather than resolving them, and smoothness is not established as more faithful to authorial intention. The main problem is exposing choices, not finding an interpretation-free performance.

passage.title: Hearing the Pause
passage.context:
A small publisher planned a spoken edition of a poet’s early notebooks. The notebooks include crossed-out words, incomplete lines, and spaces that may represent pauses or simply the end of a day’s writing. The producer wanted an actor to read the surviving words smoothly. A scholar proposed announcing each deletion and interruption. Both said they wanted listeners to encounter the notebooks rather than a finished poem that the poet had never written.

During a trial recording, the actor read one page twice. In the first version, she omitted the crossed-out words and connected a fragment to the next line. The result sounded like a continuous address. In the second, she spoke the deleted word before its replacement and paused for every blank. That version sounded like a deliberate performance of revision. The scholar recognized the difficulty: the recording made visible marks audible, but it also assigned them duration, emphasis, and intention that the page did not specify.

The publisher eventually released a reading of selected passages with brief introductions describing uncertain joins. The digital edition included images of the relevant pages and a transcript that distinguished the actor’s spoken words from the manuscript’s marks. A listener could hear a coherent reading without mistaking every pause for a command left by the poet.

The solution did not reproduce the experience of handling a notebook. Nor did it eliminate interpretation. It made some consequential choices inspectable. The producer’s smooth reading had hidden joins by passing over them; the fully annotated reading had made joins sound certain by performing them. The final edition tried to expose that problem without turning every line into a lecture about the problem.

subject: reading
questionText: What does the scholar recognize after hearing the second trial reading?
choices: Turning marks into sound adds choices not specified on the page
Sounding blanks reveals which pauses the poet intended
Speaking deleted words restores a sequence of revisions otherwise absent from the written page
Connecting fragments preserves uncertain joins more accurately than announcing them
explanation: The scholar recognizes that sounding the marks adds durations, emphasis, and intentions that the page does not specify. A blank therefore cannot automatically be identified as an intended pause. Deletions are already visible on the page; performing them does not recover an otherwise absent sequence. Nor does recognizing the second reading’s choices establish that the smooth first reading preserves uncertainty more accurately: it hides joins by passing over them.

questionText: The author would most likely consider a transcript that silently presents the actor’s pauses as the poet’s instructions:
choices: useful because consistent notation equalizes spoken choices and manuscript marks
misleading because it conceals the source of an interpretive decision
faithful because visible blanks remove the need for interpretive judgment
limited because it cannot reproduce the sound of smooth performance
explanation: The final edition distinguishes the actor’s spoken choices from manuscript marks so users can inspect their sources. Consistent notation cannot make their evidentiary status identical, and a blank does not specify pause duration or intention. The problem is attribution, not a transcript’s inability to reproduce the sound of a smooth performance.

questionText: As used in “consequential choices,” “consequential” most nearly means:

determined by the manuscript’s surviving marks

questionText: The parallel descriptions of the two trial readings in the final paragraph primarily:

subject: reading
questionText: Together, the passages mainly describe:
choices: a revision that combines familiar visual identity with clearer information
a restoration favoring regular customers’ recognition over newcomers’ need for information
a continuing dispute over how much alteration an old design can accept
a compromise preserving familiar appearance at the cost of readable information
explanation: The painter repairs the familiar name and clarifies the practical information; the owner says returning and first-time readers’ needs can share the window. Neither audience is sacrificed. The accounts describe a completed combination rather than an unresolved boundary dispute, and the familiar outline is itself treated as useful guidance rather than merely an appearance retained at the expense of reading.

passage.title: Keeping the Bakery Window
passage.context:
Passage A — A sign painter
The bakery’s old painted window was difficult to read from across the road. My first sketch replaced the curling letters with a plain typeface and enlarged the opening hours. The owner liked the clearer hours but asked me to keep the old name lettering. “Customers use that shape to find us,” she said. I traced the original carefully, repaired the missing paint, and put the practical information below it. Restoring the lettering required more work than replacing it would have. Legibility was still the aim, but I had learned that a recognizable outline can guide a reader before individual letters do.

Passage B — The bakery owner
People sometimes assume I kept the old lettering because I dislike change. I have changed the ovens, the counter, and nearly everything behind the window. The lettering is useful because our regular customers recognize it from a moving bus. A person visiting for the first time still needs to read the name and hours. The painter understood that those needs could share a window. What I opposed was a choice that treated the window as either a relic or a blank space. It was already doing a job; the new paint should help it do that job better.

subject: reading
questionText: Which part of the painter’s first sketch did the owner like?
choices: The plain name typeface
The repaired paint gaps
The clearer opening hours
The recognizable name outline
explanation: The owner likes the clearer opening hours in the first sketch but asks to keep the old name lettering. The plain name typeface is what she declines. Repairing gaps belongs to the later revision, while the recognizable outline describes the existing lettering she wants retained, not a new feature of the first sketch.

questionText: In Passage B, “relic” most nearly means:
choices: a familiar sign that continues to help people find a business
an original design restored to its first condition
an item valued only as a surviving piece of the past
a recognizable shape whose meaning depends on individual letters
explanation: Relic supplies the historical extreme of the owner’s rejected either-or choice: an object kept merely as a survivor of the past. Her point is that the window has an active present job. subject: reading
questionText: The passage mainly describes:
choices: a comparison of old and newer specimens that identifies age as the main limit on preservation
a practical investigation that uses storage location to identify and reduce a possible hazard
an experiment that establishes how closely blank paper reproduces the response of pressed leaves
a revision of handling rules intended to protect specimens from damage caused by frequent removal
explanation: The investigation follows the location of damage to a suspected low-humidity hazard, tests a preventive shield, and preserves location records. Age alone fails to explain the pattern. Paper is a practical proxy whose equivalence to leaves is explicitly limited, not the experiment’s main subject. Avoiding repeated removal protects specimens during the trial, but the revised handling rule preserves contextual evidence rather than identifying removal as the original cause.

passage.title: The Leaves in the Cabinet
passage.context:
A museum stored pressed plant specimens in cabinets lined with paper. On opening one cabinet, a technician noticed that several leaves near the door had become brittle. The oldest specimens seemed the obvious suspects, but some were intact while newer leaves had cracked. Their age alone did not explain the pattern.

The technician, Mei, mapped each damaged specimen’s position. Damage was more frequent near a heating vent that faced the cabinet door. A small sensor recorded lower humidity in that area during afternoon heating cycles. Mei proposed fitting a shield that would redirect the vent’s airflow without blocking the room’s heating. The curator approved a short trial using blank paper samples rather than moving fragile specimens repeatedly.

For two weeks, the paper samples nearest the door lost less mass on afternoons when the shield was in place. The team used mass change as an indicator of moisture loss. They did not treat the blank paper as identical to a leaf, and they did not claim that the trial would restore damage already done. It showed a way to reduce a suspected source of future stress.

The curator kept the shield and asked for continued sensor records through the next season. She also changed the cabinet’s handling instructions: staff would note where a specimen had been stored before taking it out. Mei’s map had made location useful evidence. Once a leaf was removed and its original position forgotten, that evidence could not be recovered by examining the leaf alone.

subject: reading
questionText: Why are blank paper samples used in the trial?
choices: To compare newer samples with older leaves
To avoid repeatedly moving fragile plant specimens
To apply paper’s moisture-loss rate directly to leaves
To test protection through changing storage positions
explanation: The curator approves blank paper so fragile specimens need not be moved repeatedly during the trial. The trial compares afternoons with and without the shield, not specimen ages or a treatment based on changing storage positions. Mass change is an indicator of moisture loss in the paper; the team explicitly does not assume that paper behaves identically to a leaf.

passage.title: The Leaves in the Cabinet
passage.context:
A museum stored pressed plant specimens in cabinets lined with paper. On opening one cabinet, a technician noticed that several leaves near the door had become brittle. The oldest specimens seemed the obvious suspects, but some were intact while newer leaves had cracked. Their age alone did not explain the pattern.

The technician, Mei, mapped each damaged specimen’s position. Damage was more frequent near a heating vent that faced the cabinet door. She also changed the cabinet’s handling instructions: staff would note where a specimen had been stored before taking it out. Mei’s map had made location useful evidence. Once a leaf was removed and its original position forgotten, that evidence could not be recovered by examining the leaf alone.

questionText: Taken together, the passages argue that trust in a model requires attention to:
choices: the accuracy of its fit to the best-documented storm and clarity of that single comparison
the stability of local forecasts across plausible inputs despite changes in the citywide total
both performance beyond the events used to tune it and uncertainty relevant to particular decisions
both unused-storm accuracy and selection of a conservative boundary applicable to every evacuation decision
explanation: A requires tests beyond the event used for adjustment, with errors visible; B adds uncertainty at the scale where a decision may change. A single well-reported fit is not enough. B does not require predictions to remain identical across plausible inputs: disagreement can itself prompt an alternative route. B also explicitly rejects hiding uncertainty in one worst-case map, so unused-storm testing alone does not justify a single boundary for every decision.

passage.title: Two Ways to Trust a Flood Model
passage.context:
Passage A — Model developer
We should not judge the new flood model solely by how closely it reproduces one famous storm. A model can be adjusted until it fits a single event beautifully and still fail under different rainfall patterns. We tested the same settings against several earlier storms that had not been used in adjustment. The results were imperfect but generally captured which districts flooded first. I would publish those comparisons and their errors. A visible error range is more useful for planning than an exact-looking line whose reliability has been demonstrated only where it was tuned.

Passage B — Emergency planner
Testing against unused storms is necessary, but a model’s usefulness also depends on the decision being made. An error that barely changes a citywide total can move a predicted flood boundary across a care home’s access road. For evacuation planning, I need to see how plausible changes in the inputs alter that local prediction. If several reasonable versions disagree, the disagreement itself may justify preparing an alternative route. I am not asking the developer to hide uncertainty in a single worst-case map. I am asking for uncertainty to be expressed where it can change an action.

The model estimates flood extent from rainfall, ground conditions, and drainage information. Neither writer claims that earlier storms cover every future possibility. Both support making limits visible rather than presenting one unqualified forecast.

questionText: The passage mainly describes:
choices: a higher completion rate that confirms the notebook has resolved the shortage of parts
a change that improves repair preparation while leaving reasons for unfinished work worth tracking
a repair queue reordered according to the parts available at the April event
an effort to compare events by counting diagnoses instead of jointly tested repairs
explanation: The notebook helps prepare parts, but organizers retain records of unfinished work and acknowledge other possible differences between events. The increase does not establish that the shortage is resolved. Ticket order still governs first examination, and a completed repair still requires joint testing rather than a diagnosis.

passage.title: The Repair Queue
passage.context:
At a neighborhood repair morning, every broken appliance received a numbered ticket. The numbers established the order in which volunteers first examined items. A quick examination did not guarantee a completed repair: some items required a part that the volunteers did not have, and others needed more time than the event allowed.

In March, organizers began a parts notebook. When a repair could not proceed, the volunteer wrote down the missing part and, with the owner’s permission, a way to contact the owner. Before the April event, a local shop donated several commonly requested parts. The organizers did not change ticket order or promise that every item could be fixed.

The table records items first examined and items repaired during those two mornings. An item counted as repaired only if its owner and a volunteer tested it together before leaving. Items awaiting parts were not counted as repairs, even if a volunteer had identified the problem.

After April, one organizer said that the notebook had solved the parts problem. Another was pleased by the increase but wanted to keep recording the items that still could not be repaired. More parts were available, yet the mix of appliances and the volunteers present could also differ between events. They agreed to keep the notebook and add a column for the reason a repair remained unfinished.

questionText: The central concern shared by the passages is:
choices: whether visitors’ reports are more reliable than residents’ reports
how a sound map’s usefulness depends on the question and evidence behind it
how a survey should balance the convenience of audience seating against complaints from nearby homes
whether the reach of bass rhythms can be predicted from measurements of the speakers
explanation: A defends a clear-hearing map for seating, while B accepts that use and objects to extending it to all sound. Both connect a map’s interpretation to its question and evidence. They do not rank visitors’ honesty against residents’ honesty or weigh seating benefits against complaints. Neither passage proposes predicting bass from speaker measurements; the original survey contains no sound-level measurements.

passage.title: How Wide Is a Sound Map?
passage.context:
Passage A — A festival organizer
Last year we asked visitors to mark where they could hear the outdoor stage clearly. Their dots formed a small oval in front of the speakers. We used that map to position this year’s seating. It served its purpose: people who wanted to hear the performance could choose a place with less guesswork. The map was never intended to describe every effect of the stage on the neighborhood. Asking it to do so would confuse one useful tool with a different investigation.

Passage B — A resident and survey designer
The seating map answered a real question, but the council later displayed it under the heading “Where festival sound reaches.” That broader label was not supported by the survey. People could hear a faint bass rhythm at home without hearing the words clearly. Some residents who heard it did not attend the festival and never received a dot to place. I would keep the seating map with its original question stated beside it. For the council’s question, I would ask about different kinds of audibility at different locations and times, including experiences outside the audience. A map’s boundary can mark the boundary of a question rather than the boundary of a phenomenon.

The original survey asked only people attending the festival to mark places where the performance was clear enough to follow. It did not include sound-level measurements.

Last year we asked visitors to mark where they could hear the outdoor stage clearly. Their dots formed a small oval in front of the speakers. We used that map to position this year’s seating. It served its purpose: people who wanted to hear the performance could choose a place with less guesswork. The map was never intended to describe every effect of the stage on the neighborhood. Asking it to do so would confuse one useful tool with a different investigation.

The seating map answered a real question, but the council later displayed it under the heading “Where festival sound reaches.” That broader label was not supported by the survey.
